about.what: Checked facts for SafeCrop's advice. Gemini rewrites these in plain words; it must not add treatments.
rules: No chemical names and no doses. Say: ask your local agriculture officer which product and dose to use.
Every entry needs 1-3 sources. Set 'checked' to true only after a person has opened every source and compared the facts.

helpline.name: Krishi Call Centre (Department of Agricultural Extension, DAE)
helpline.note: Calls go to agriculture officers. Also: your Upazila Agriculture Office.

about.ask_officer: Ask your local agriculture officer which product and dose to use.

entries.cause: A water mould called Phytophthora infestans. It spreads very fast in cool, wet or foggy weather.
entries.short: Dark, wet-looking patches on potato leaves that spread fast in cool, damp weather and can kill the whole plant.
signs: Pale or dark green, wet-looking spots, often at the tips and edges of leaves, with a yellow ring around them.
The spots grow quickly into large dark brown patches that are not stopped by the leaf veins.
In damp weather, a white, fuzzy growth on the underside of the leaf at the edge of the spots.
Dark patches on the leaf stalks and stems; whole plants can turn brown and dry as if burnt by frost.
Potatoes in the ground can get reddish-brown, dry rot under the skin.
do_now: Check the whole field today, especially after fog or rain. The disease can strip a field in about two weeks.
Pull out badly sick plants, put them in a bag or bury them deep. Do not leave them in a heap near the field.
Keep the leaves as dry as you can: water the soil, not the leaves, and water in the morning.
Spraying can protect the healthy plants, but timing matters. Ask your local agriculture officer which product and dose to use.
prevention: Plant clean, certified seed potatoes, and a resistant variety if one is available.
Remove volunteer potato plants and piles of thrown-away potatoes, where the disease survives.
Leave space between plants so air can move and leaves dry quickly.
Cover the potatoes well with soil (earthing up) so spores from the leaves don't reach them.
Harvest in dry weather and store only healthy potatoes.
entries.see_expert_when: Call an expert at once if many plants show spots after foggy or rainy days, or if spots keep spreading after you removed sick plants.
looks_like: Potato early blight (round brown spots with rings like a target)

sources.title: Late blight of tomato and potato — University of Minnesota Extension
Late Blight / Potato — UC Statewide IPM Program
Tomato-Potato Late Blight in the Home Garden — Penn State Extension

entries.cause: A fungus called Venturia inaequalis. It lives through the winter in fallen leaves and spreads in wet spring weather.
entries.short: Olive-green to dark brown, velvety spots on apple leaves and rough, cracked spots on the fruit.
signs: Small, olive-green spots that later turn brown or black, often first on the underside of the leaf.
The spots have a soft, feathery edge and a velvety look.
Badly hit leaves turn yellow and fall early.
Dark, rough (scabby) spots on the fruit that crack as the fruit grows; young fruit can be bent out of shape.
do_now: Pick up and remove fallen leaves under the tree; this is where the fungus survives.
Remove badly spotted fruit so it does not spread the disease.
Sprays work only if they are on time and cover both sides of the leaves. Ask your local agriculture officer which product and dose to use.
prevention: Clean up fallen leaves in autumn or early spring (rake them up, bury or compost them).
Prune the tree so air and sun reach inside and leaves dry fast.
Choose scab-resistant apple varieties when planting new trees.
entries.see_expert_when: Ask an expert if spots appear on many leaves and fruit early in the season, or if spots come back every year.

entries.cause: This is an insect pest, not a disease. The caterpillar (larva) of a small moth, mostly the yellow stem borer (Scirpophaga incertulas), eats the inside of the rice stem.
entries.short: An insect, not a disease: its caterpillars bore into rice stems, so the centre shoot dies (dead heart) or the panicle comes out white and empty (white head).
signs: Dead heart: in young plants the centre leaf rolls, turns brown and dries; it pulls out easily by hand.
White head: at flowering time the panicle turns white and the grains are empty.
Small holes in the stem and the caterpillar or its waste inside the stem.
Small groups of eggs, covered with light brown hairs, near the tips of the leaves.
Small yellowish-white moths flying at night, attracted to lights.
do_now: Pull out plants with dead hearts and destroy them, with the caterpillar inside.
Collect and destroy egg groups from the leaf tips.
Put bamboo sticks or branches in the field so birds can sit there and eat the moths and caterpillars (perching).
Once white heads have appeared it is too late for a spray to help that crop.
Use an insecticide only if an officer says the number of insects is high enough. Ask your local agriculture officer which product and dose to use.
prevention: After harvest, cut the stubble close to the ground and plough the field to kill caterpillars hiding in it.
Plant at the same time as your neighbours, so the insects don't move from field to field.
Use the variety and planting time your local office recommends.
Do not use too much nitrogen fertiliser (urea); soft, lush plants attract more borers.
entries.see_expert_when: Ask an expert if you see dead hearts or egg groups in many hills, or white heads spreading around the field.

entries.cause: A virus (mungbean yellow mosaic virus and related viruses). Tiny white flies (whitefly) carry it from sick plants to healthy ones. It is not spread by seed or by touch.
entries.short: Bright yellow and green patches (a mosaic) on black gram leaves, spread by whitefly; plants give few, small pods.
signs: Small yellow spots on young leaves that grow into bright yellow and green patches (a mosaic).
Later, whole leaves can turn yellow.
Sick plants stay small and give few pods; pods are small, bent, and can also have yellow patches.
Plants infected when young may die before making seed.
Tiny white insects (whitefly) on the underside of the leaves.
do_now: Pull out sick plants early (in the first weeks after sowing) and destroy them away from the field.
Hang yellow sticky traps to catch whitefly.
Remove weeds in and around the field; they can hide the virus and the whitefly.
There is no cure for a plant that already has the virus. To control whitefly, ask your local agriculture officer which product and dose to use.
prevention: Grow a resistant variety; ask your local office which one is recommended in your area.
Sow at the recommended time.
Keep the field and its edges free of weeds.
Some farmers grow a few rows of a tall crop (maize or sorghum) around the field as a barrier against whitefly.
entries.see_expert_when: Ask an expert if many young plants show yellow patches, or if whitefly numbers are high.

sources.title: Black gram: Yellow mosaic — TNAU Agritech Portal
Yellow mosaic of mungbean and urdbean: current status and future strategies (FAO AGRIS record)

entries.cause: A fungus called Septoria pyricola (also called Mycosphaerella pyri). It lives in fallen leaves and spreads with rain.
entries.short: Small round spots with a grey-white centre and a dark purple-brown edge on pear leaves.
signs: Small round spots, about 3–5 mm across, first on the upper side of the leaf.
Each spot has a grey or whitish centre and a dark brown or purple edge.
Tiny black dots inside older spots.
Many spots can make leaves yellow and fall early, mostly late in the season.
Sometimes small dark spots on the fruit.
do_now: Remove and destroy fallen leaves under the tree.
Remove badly spotted leaves you can reach.
If many leaves are spotted, ask your local agriculture officer which product and dose to use.
prevention: Clean up fallen leaves every season; the fungus survives in them.
Prune the tree so air moves and leaves dry quickly after rain.
Water the soil, not the leaves.
entries.see_expert_when: Ask an expert if spots cover many leaves or leaves are falling early.
looks_like: Fabraea leaf spot of pear (darker spots)

sources.title: Pear Leaf Spot in the Home Fruit Planting — Penn State Extension
Mycosphaerella leaf spot — Michigan State University IPM
DiaMOS Plant dataset description (our photo source; lists Septoria piricola)

entries.cause: A fungus called Pseudocercospora vitis (old name Isariopsis), so it is also called Isariopsis leaf spot.
entries.short: Brown to purplish-brown spots on grape leaves, often on older leaves late in the season; badly hit leaves dry and fall.
signs: Brown or purplish-brown spots on the upper side of the leaf, round or uneven, a few millimetres across.
Spots can join into larger dead (dry) areas.
Later, dark growth on the underside of the leaf below the spots.
Mostly older leaves; badly hit leaves dry up and fall early.
do_now: Remove spotted leaves and fallen leaves and destroy them away from the vines.
Keep the leaves dry: water the soil, not the leaves.
If many leaves are spotted, ask your local agriculture officer which product and dose to use.
prevention: Clean up fallen leaves after the season.
Prune and train the vines so air moves through them.
In well-looked-after vineyards this disease is seldom a big problem.
entries.see_expert_when: Ask an expert if spots spread over many vines or leaves fall early.

sources.title: Leaf spots of grapes — University of Kentucky Fruit Scouting Guide
Pseudocercospora vitis (MYCOPS) — EPPO Global Database

entries.cause: A virus (a begomovirus) carried by tiny white flies (whitefly). In Bangladesh it is reported as one of the most damaging jute diseases.
entries.short: Yellow and green patches (a mosaic) on jute leaves, spread by whitefly; it lowers fibre yield and quality.
signs: Small yellow flecks on young leaves.
The flecks grow into mixed yellow and green patches (a mosaic).
Leaves can become wrinkled or smaller, and plants grow less.
Tiny white insects (whitefly) on the underside of the leaves.
do_now: Pull out sick plants early and destroy them away from the field.
Remove weeds in and around the field.
Hang yellow sticky traps to catch whitefly.
There is no cure for a plant that already has the virus. To control whitefly, ask your local agriculture officer which product and dose to use.
prevention: Use healthy seed of a variety your local office or BJRI recommends.
Keep the field and its edges free of weeds.
Check young plants often for yellow flecks and whitefly.
entries.see_expert_when: Ask an expert if many plants show yellow patches, or whitefly numbers are high.

Jute — Banglapedia

entries.cause: The plant dies from the tip downwards. In research it is a later stage of fungus attacks on the stem, best described for jute anthracnose (Colletotrichum fungi). The exact cause for our photos is not confirmed.
entries.short: Jute leaves and shoot tips turn brown and dry from the top down; often a later stage of a fungus attack on the stem.
signs: Leaves near the top of the plant turn brown and dry.
The shoot tip and side branches wither and die back from the top.
Dark brown or black, sunken patches on the stem.
Leaves fall early.
do_now: Cut off and destroy dried tips and badly sick plants, away from the field.
Do not leave sick plant parts in the field or in the water used for retting nearby.
Ask your local agriculture officer which product and dose to use, if any treatment is needed.
prevention: Use healthy, clean seed from a trusted source.
Keep good drainage so water does not stand around the plants.
Remove plant remains after harvest and rotate crops.
entries.see_expert_when: Ask an expert soon: several fungi cause similar damage on jute, and an expert can tell which one it is.

sources.title: Anthracnose of jute (Colletotrichum) — Scientific Reports (PMC4848545)
Jute — Banglapedia

entries.short: The leaf looks like the healthy leaves in our pictures.
signs: Even green colour, without spots, patches or a yellow mosaic.
No dry, brown tips or edges.
No holes and no insects on the leaf.
do_now: Nothing to treat now. Keep checking your plants once or twice a week.
Check again after rain, fog or a spell of cool, damp weather, when many diseases spread.
prevention: Use healthy seed and keep the field free of weeds.
Give plants space so air moves and leaves dry quickly.
Remove sick plants as soon as you see them.
entries.see_expert_when: Ask an expert if the plant looks weak or grows badly even though the leaves look healthy.

entries.short: The leaf looks most like a disease SafeCrop does not cover, so SafeCrop cannot give advice for it.
do_now: Do not spray anything until you know what the problem is.
Take a clear photo of the leaf and show it, or the plant, to your local agriculture officer.
You can also call the Krishi Call Centre at 16123.
prevention: Remove badly sick leaves or plants so the problem does not spread.
Keep the field clean and free of weeds.
entries.see_expert_when: Ask an expert now: SafeCrop only knows 8 problems and this may be a different one.
